low-taper-fade: The silhouette follows the shape of the skull rather than ballooning out from it.
buzz-cut: Cut this much shorter than a short crop: one uniform clipper grade, roughly three millimetres, over the entire head — top, sides and back all the same length, with no longer section anywhere. The scalp reads clearly through the hair as a shadow rather than as a solid mass of strands, and the silhouette sits tight against the skull with no bulk, no volume and no styled shape above it. No fringe and no edged-up hairline: the front hairline is a soft, natural fade into the forehead, not a drawn line. No sideburns beyond a faint shadow at the ear, and the taper at the nape is the same shaved length as the rest.
afro:
An afro is defined by the hair standing out and away from the scalp in every direction and holding a rounded, close-to-spherical halo around the head. It is not a short natural lying flat against the skull, not a rounded cap following the shape of the skull, and not hair that hangs down.

Size it by measurement, not by impression. At the cut's normal, default length the mass stands clear of the skull by about half a head-width on every side and rises about half a head-height above the crown, so the whole silhouette is roughly one and a half times as wide and one and a half times as tall as the bare head. The widest point of the hair is level with or above the eyeline and sits far outside the line of the ears; the ears and the nape are buried inside the mass rather than showing below it. This is a big, full, statement afro at its default length — the size a picked-out afro is worn at, not a modest one — and that is the normal length for this cut, not its long version.

Where several lengths are shown, the halo keeps that shape and only its radius changes: a shorter afro still stands clear of the scalp on every side, by about a quarter of a head-width, and a longer one stands clear by about a full head-width. At no length does it flatten against the skull, part, or collapse into hair that hangs down past the jaw.

The mass is even all the way round and densely packed, with no parting anywhere, no fringe, no scalp showing through and no section falling over the ears or onto the shoulders. Its outer edge is soft and slightly diffuse rather than a hard sculpted outline. Seen from the front, the three-quarter, the side or the back, the outline is a circle centred on the head, and the head reads as sitting inside the hair rather than wearing a cap of it.

When this cut is named as the men's version it is the same halo at the same size, worn by a man — not a barbered short natural. The sides and the back are not cut back, tapered, faded or shortened against the top: the hair is the same length all over and stands out from the head just as far at the sides and the back as it does on top, so the outline stays a circle rather than a dome sitting on close-cut sides. There is no taper at the nape, no line-up or shaved edge at the temple or the forehead, and no straight hard edge anywhere along the hairline — the front edge of the hair is soft and diffuse, never a band ruled across the forehead.

A tighter coil pattern does not mean a smaller afro. The hair is picked out with an afro pick so that the coils are lifted and expanded away from the scalp into the round halo described above: the tighter the coil, the more it is picked out. Type 4 coils in particular must not be drawn as a short, dense cap sitting on the skull — that is a close-cropped natural, which is a different haircut. The whole point of this cut is the volume, at every length.
two-block-cut: Two clearly separate blocks with a visible step between them, never a blended fade. The sides and the back are clipped to a short, uniform length from the temple and the nape up to a horizontal line level with the top of the ear. Above that line the hair is left long and heavy and overhangs the clipped section, so the outline has a distinct ledge where the two lengths meet and the upper block casts a shadow onto the lower one. There is no taper and no gradient anywhere along that line. The top is worn forward into a fringe that reaches the eyebrows.
comma-hair: The fringe is the whole subject. It is blow-dried forward off a side parting and the individual strands hook inward at the ends into a comma shape, curving down and then back toward the centre of the forehead, so each piece reads as a separate tapered stroke with a rounded head and a thin tail. The fringe reaches the eyebrows and splits into two or three of these comma strokes rather than hanging as a flat curtain; there is visible separation and air between them. The hair lifts at the root before it curves, so the fringe stands away from the forehead rather than lying on it. The sides are short and flat against the head so nothing competes with the fringe.
korean-perm: A loose, soft perm, not a tight curl and not a wave set. The top and the fringe are lifted into rounded, irregular bends about the width of two fingers, giving height at the crown and movement through the fringe, with the ends left soft rather than defined. The sides and the back stay short and lie flat against the head — the volume is only on top, so the silhouette is a soft rounded mass sitting above flat sides. The fringe falls to the eyebrow in loose separated pieces.
mash-cut: A rounded, full shape: seen from the front the outline is a smooth curve with no corners, and the hair covers the top halves of the ears rather than being cut back from them. The length is even all the way round the perimeter, falling to about the middle of the ear at the sides and to the nape at the back, so the whole cut reads as one soft dome sitting on the head. The fringe is straight, full and cut level across the eyebrows. There is no undercut, no fade, no taper and no disconnection anywhere — the sides continue smoothly from the top. The ends are soft and lightly point-cut, not a hard blunt bowl edge.
hime-cut: Three straight lines and nothing else, cut with hard blunt edges. First, a blunt straight fringe cut level across the eyebrows with a hard horizontal edge and no thinning or feathering. Second, on each side of the face, a separate panel of hair cut straight down and ended in a hard horizontal edge at cheekbone level, level with the bottom of the nose, so the panel sits in front of the ear and is clearly shorter than everything behind it. That side panel is the defining feature and must be plainly visible from the front and the three-quarter view as a step in the outline. Third, the rest of the hair is left long, straight and uncut, falling past the bottom edge of the frame. All three edges are geometric and razor-clean. This is a hairstyle only: no ornaments, no headwear, no costume, no accessories of any kind.
hush-cut: Long, soft, airy layers with visible separation between the pieces. The layers start around the cheekbone at the face and continue through the length, cut so the hair falls open and away from the face rather than sitting as one solid mass. The ends are heavily point-cut and wispy, never blunt. The overall length reaches the collarbone. The face-framing pieces are the shortest and the rest graduates gently behind them. The finish is soft and undone, with air and gaps visible through the layers, not sleek and not sculpted.
see-through-bangs: A deliberately sparse fringe. It is cut thin enough that the forehead is clearly visible through it — the skin shows between the strands across the whole width of the fringe, not just at the edges. The hair is split into fine separated wisps with gaps between them rather than cut as a solid curtain, and it falls flat against the forehead to about the middle of the eyebrow. It is not a full blunt fringe, not a curtain fringe parted in the centre, and not swept to one side. The rest of the hair is left long and straight and simply continues past the bottom edge of the frame.
c-curl-perm: Only the ends are permed. The roots, the crown and most of the length are left completely straight and flat; in the last few inches the hair curves inward toward the neck in one wide, open C-shaped bend, so the ends turn under and in rather than out. It is a single gentle curve, not a curl, not a spiral and not a wave — there is exactly one bend per section and it happens near the bottom. Seen from the front, the ends tuck in toward the jaw on both sides; seen from the back they turn under in a smooth continuous curve. The length reaches the collarbone.
